question_text: A colleague sitting near you is clearly not going to finish an important task by tomorrow. Your own work is on track. What would you most likely do?
option_a: Take part of their workload onto your own plate.
option_b: Walk through the problem with them so they can finish it themselves.
option_c: Tell your lead that the deadline is at risk.
option_d: Stay on your own work — their deadline is theirs to manage.

question_text: You finish your own tasks for the day early. Someone else on the same project is visibly behind on theirs. What do you do?
option_a: Ask what is blocking them and work through it with them.
option_b: Say nothing — they will ask if they want a hand.
option_c: Pick up whichever of their items you can finish yourself.
option_d: Mention the slippage to whoever is running the project.

question_text: A week after you signed it off, you spot an error in a figure that has already gone to the client. What do you do?
option_a: Tell the client and your lead straight away.
option_b: Correct it quietly and mention it only if someone asks.
option_c: Fix it first, then tell your lead once it is sorted.
option_d: Wait and see whether anyone notices.

question_text: A defect you introduced has reached production. Nobody has connected it to you yet. What do you do?
option_a: Say nothing unless it gets traced back to you.
option_b: Put your hand up immediately and explain what happened.
option_c: Resolve it, then report it as already handled.
option_d: Push a fix without drawing attention to where it came from.

question_text: A meeting has drifted for twenty minutes with nobody chairing it. What would you most likely do?
option_a: Step in and put some structure on the discussion.
option_b: Suggest that the most senior person in the room takes it over.
option_c: Contribute when asked and let it run its course.
option_d: Wait for it to end and raise your points separately.

question_text: A project has kicked off with nobody clearly responsible for coordinating it. What do you do?
option_a: Get on with your own part and let coordination sort itself out.
option_c: Raise it with your manager and ask them to appoint someone.
option_d: Keep your head down until somebody is named.

option_a: Ship on Friday with a few rough edges left in.
option_b: Ship on Tuesday with everything checked.

question_text: A client asks whether you could deliver a week earlier than planned. Which would you rather do?
option_a: Hold the original date and hand over something fully tested.
option_b: Take the earlier date and drop the optional checks.

question_text: On the morning of your deadline your priorities are rewritten, and the deadline still stands. What do you do?
option_a: Re-plan the day and get on with the new list.
option_b: Ask which of the two you are actually being measured on.
option_c: Push back and ask for the deadline to move.
option_d: Carry on with the original plan and hope it still counts.

question_text: You are halfway through a piece of work when the requirements change substantially. What do you do?
option_a: Finish what you started — the new version can be a second pass.
option_b: Go back and confirm what success looks like now.
option_c: Rework it to the new requirements and keep moving.
option_d: Ask for more time before you change anything.

question_text: In a meeting, someone far more senior than you states something you know to be factually wrong. What do you do?
option_a: Correct it there and then, politely.
option_b: Raise it with them privately afterwards.
option_c: Mention it to a peer first and see whether they agree.
option_d: Leave it — it is not your place to correct them.

question_text: Your manager presents a plan with a flaw you appear to be the only person to have spotted. What do you do?
option_a: Keep it to yourself — they will find out soon enough.
option_b: Catch them one to one and set the problem out.
option_c: Say it in the room, while everyone can hear the answer.
option_d: Sound out a colleague before you say anything.

question_text: Your team's work is praised in front of the department, and only your name is mentioned. What do you do?
option_a: Name the people who actually did the work.
option_b: Say you will come back to it, then thank them privately.
option_c: Accept it — correcting people in public is awkward.
option_d: Say nothing and let the impression stand.

question_text: Work your whole team delivered has failed, and leadership asks who was responsible. What do you do?
option_a: Let the question hang — somebody else will answer it.
option_b: Say the team delivered it and you were part of that team.
option_c: Name the person whose step actually failed.
option_d: Say you will come back with a full account of what happened.

question_text: You can choose your next piece of work. Which do you take?
option_a: The safe one, where you already know the ground.
option_b: The unfamiliar one, where you would be learning as you go.
